findings.source_passage: no face; he has none, proper; nothing but that one broad firmament of a forehead, pleated with riddles; dumbly lowering with the doom of boats, and ships, and men.
findings.source_locator: paragraph on the brow / full front view
findings.why_it_matters: The draft wraps the passage in quotation marks as if citing a source rather than delivering it in Ishmael's own first-person voice, and omits the crucial build-up ('no nose, eyes, ears, or mouth; no face; he has none, proper') that makes the rhetorical climax land. The quotation-mark framing is a fabrication that misattributes the narrator's own prose.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove the quotation marks and restore the full anaphoric list: 'no nose, eyes, ears, or mouth; no face; he has none, proper; nothing but that one broad firmament of a forehead, pleated with riddles; dumbly lowering with the doom of boats, and ships, and men.'

findings.source_passage: his great genius is declared in his doing nothing particular to prove it. It is moreover declared in his pyramidical silence.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'But how? Genius in the Sperm Whale?'
findings.why_it_matters: The opening rhetorical question 'But how? Genius in the Sperm Whale? Has the Sperm Whale ever written a book, spoken a speech?' is a critically noted ironic flourish that carries interpretive weight about Melville's conception of nonhuman sublimity; flattening it to 'Genius? He has written no book' strips the Socratic irony and register.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full rhetorical question sequence: 'But how? Genius in the Sperm Whale? Has the Sperm Whale ever written a book, spoken a speech? No, his great genius is declared in his doing nothing particular to prove it.'

findings.source_passage: if hereafter any highly cultured, poetical nation shall lure back to their birth-right, the merry May-day gods of old; and livingly enthrone them again in the now egotistical sky; in the now unhaunted hill
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'But how? Genius in the Sperm Whale?', closing sentences
findings.why_it_matters: This visionary, syntactically distinctive passage about restoring the 'merry May-day gods' to the 'now egotistical sky' is one of Melville's most characteristic prophetic-ironic asides; it is entirely omitted, replaced by a compressed paraphrase that loses both the mythology and the register.
findings.suggested_fix: Re-insert the conditional vision: 'if hereafter any highly cultured, poetical nation shall lure back to their birth-right, the merry May-day gods of old; and livingly enthrone them again in the now egotistical sky; in the now unhaunted hill; then be sure, exalted to Jove's high seat, the great Sperm Whale shall lord it.'

findings.source_passage: Champollion deciphered the wrinkled granite hieroglyphics. But there is no Champollion to decipher the Egypt of every man's and every being's face.
findings.why_it_matters: The opening of the final paragraph drops the Champollion sentence that sets up the Egypt metaphor, jumping directly to 'there is no Champollion'; the antithetical structure (he deciphered granite — but no one can decipher a face) is weakened.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the lead sentence: 'Champollion deciphered the wrinkled granite hieroglyphics. But there is no Champollion to decipher the Egypt of every man's and every being's face.'

summary: Three medium-severity failures — the misattributed-quotation-mark framing of the 'firmament of a forehead' climax, the erasure of the 'But how? Genius in the Sperm Whale?' ironic-question sequence, and the complete omission of the 'merry May-day gods / now egotistical sky' visionary aside — collectively constitute enough voice erasure and interpretive loss to require regeneration.
